name: Jet.AI Inc.

profile.description: Jet.AI Inc. is a micro-cap company pivoting from AI-powered private aviation software to AI data center infrastructure. Founded in 2018 by Mike Winston and currently led by CEO George Murnane, the company developed CharterGPT (AI-powered natural language jet booking), Reroute AI (aircraft repositioning optimization), and DynoFlight (emissions tracking API). In July 2026, stockholders approved the divestiture of the aviation business to flyExclusive, pivoting the company toward a 50MW data center project. JTAI has undergone two massive reverse stock splits — 1:225 in November 2024 and 1:200 in April 2026 — to maintain NASDAQ listing compliance. With a market cap of $2.64M, 1.42M shares outstanding, and an Altman Z-score of -0.58 indicating elevated bankruptcy risk, the company is in severe financial distress. Q1 2026 EPS of -$6.68 missed estimates by 234%. The 52-week stock price decline of 99.7% reflects the market's assessment of the company's viability.

innovation.label: WEAK
innovation.analysis: Track Record (1/3): Jet.AI developed CharterGPT, an AI-powered natural language processing app for private jet booking, along with Reroute AI and DynoFlight products [2]. These represent modest product development in the private aviation niche but achieved minimal commercial traction — total company revenue is only $7.38M TTM, and the aviation business is being divested to flyExclusive [1]. No evidence of successful product launches that opened significant new revenue streams. AI Deployment (1/2): CharterGPT uses NLP and machine learning to improve the private jet booking experience, and DynoFlight enables emissions tracking via API — these are shipping AI products, though with minimal revenue impact and unclear customer adoption metrics [2]. Market Share (0/2): No meaningful market share in any category. The company's $2.64M market cap makes it one of the smallest public companies, with negligible presence in either private aviation software or data centers [4]. Product Pipeline (0/2): The company signed a letter of intent for a 50MW data center project, but no specific construction timelines, customer commitments, or revenue projections have been disclosed [2]. The pivot from aviation to data centers is aspirational with no concrete product roadmap. R&D Intensity (0/1): No data on R&D spending. As a company with only $7.38M in total revenue and ~30 employees, R&D investment is negligible in absolute terms.

inspiration.label: WEAK
inspiration.analysis: Mission Floor (1/4): Jet.AI describes itself as 'a business-to-business software platform for SaaS products and private aviation services' — a functional description rather than an inspiring purpose [2]. The recent pivot to 'AI Data Center Infrastructure' offers no articulated vision for why the company exists beyond generating revenue. The company's purpose appears to shift with each business model pivot, from private aviation to data centers, suggesting an absence of an enduring mission. Community Impact (0/2): No evidence of charitable giving, community programs, or social impact initiatives. The company's micro-cap status and financial distress leave no capacity for community investment. Employee Retention (0/2): No employee retention or tenure data is publicly available. With approximately 30 employees and a company undergoing a complete business model pivot, workforce stability is highly uncertain. Insider Buying (0/2): No evidence of insider buying. The company's multiple reverse splits (1:225 and 1:200) and 99.7% stock price decline suggest insiders are not putting their own capital at risk [3].

infrastructure.label: STRONG
infrastructure.analysis: CAUTION: This mechanically calculated score significantly overestimates JTAI's financial health. The reported ROE of 20.48% and profit margin of 68.77% are entirely distorted by a one-time gain from the flyExclusive aviation business divestiture, not from ongoing operations [1]. On an operating basis, Q1 2026 showed EPS of -$6.68 on revenue of $1.68M, implying annualized operating losses of approximately -$38M — deeply negative margins. The only reliably positive metric is D/E of 1% (minimal debt), which scores perfectly [4]. Revenue growth YoY of approximately -15% scores 0.17 as the aviation business winds down ahead of the flyExclusive divestiture. The company's $2.64M market cap, Altman Z-score of -0.58, 99.7% 52-week stock decline, and two reverse splits in 18 months paint a picture of a company in severe financial distress that the mechanically calculated Infrastructure score of 8 does not reflect [3][4].

ai_resilience.label: HIGH RISK
ai_resilience.analysis: AI Risk Protection (4/9): JTAI occupies an awkward position — the company IS attempting to be an AI company (CharterGPT, Reroute AI) while also pivoting to physical data center infrastructure. The aviation software business faces significant AI disruption risk from larger, better-funded competitors building AI-powered booking and operations platforms. The planned 50MW data center, if built, would provide physical infrastructure that is immune to AI disruption, but a single 50MW facility is trivially small compared to competitors deploying gigawatts of capacity (IREN has 3GW) [2]. The company has no competitive moat in either software or infrastructure — no proprietary data, no scale advantages, no regulatory protection, and no switching costs. The $2.64M market cap reflects a company with no meaningful defensive position against any form of competition, AI or otherwise [4]. AI Opportunity (0/1): While CharterGPT and Reroute AI are technically AI products, they generate negligible revenue within the $7.38M TTM total, and the aviation business is being divested. No quantifiable AI revenue that meets the threshold for this tiebreaker point [1].

infinite_game.summary: Jet.AI exhibits no characteristics of an infinite game player. The company has no articulated Just Cause, no evidence of courageous leadership decisions, no indicators of organizational trust, and is pivoting between business models in what appears to be survival mode rather than mission-driven strategic evolution. The two reverse stock splits, 99.7% stock decline, and business divestiture suggest a company playing a finite game it is losing.

just_cause.analysis: Just Cause (0/3): No Just Cause is evident. The company's purpose has shifted from private aviation software to data center infrastructure, with no articulated vision of a better future that connects these disparate business models [2]. The strategic pivot appears driven by financial necessity (the aviation business was unprofitable) rather than a cause that demands the pivot. Sinek would identify this as a company that exists to survive rather than to advance a purpose — the classic finite player.

trusting_teams.analysis: Trusting Teams (0/2): No evidence of team culture, employee empowerment, or organizational trust. With approximately 30 employees and a complete business model pivot underway, organizational stability is questionable. The leadership transition from founder Mike Winston to CEO George Murnane, combined with the flyExclusive divestiture and data center pivot, suggests significant internal disruption. No Glassdoor reviews or employee sentiment data is available to assess the organizational environment.

worthy_rivals.analysis: Worthy Rivals (0/1): No evidence of competitive self-reflection or acknowledgment of rivals' strengths. The company is too small ($2.64M market cap) and too distressed to engage in meaningful competitive positioning. In both the aviation software and data center infrastructure markets, JTAI is dwarfed by competitors with thousands of times more resources.

existential_flexibility.analysis: Existential Flexibility (0/2): While JTAI is pivoting from aviation software to data center infrastructure, Sinek's Existential Flexibility requires the pivot to be 'in service of the Just Cause.' JTAI has no Just Cause — the pivot appears to be survival-driven, chasing the data center and AI infrastructure trend because the aviation business failed to achieve viability [2]. This is adaptation by necessity, not the transformative, cause-driven flexibility that characterizes infinite game players. Sinek would likely view this as desperation masquerading as flexibility.

courage_to_lead.analysis: Courage to Lead (0/2): No evidence of leadership making costly long-term investments in service of a vision. The two reverse stock splits (1:225 and 1:200) represent financial engineering to maintain NASDAQ listing compliance, not courageous strategic decisions [3]. The flyExclusive divestiture is a retreat from an unprofitable business, and the 50MW data center LOI is an aspirational announcement without demonstrated capital commitment. Leadership decisions appear reactive to circumstances rather than proactive in service of a long-term vision.

investment_thesis: JTAI has no credible investment thesis at current fundamentals. The company's $2.64M market cap, $7.38M TTM revenue, Q1 2026 EPS of -$6.68 (missing estimates by 234%), and two reverse stock splits in 18 months reflect a company in acute financial distress [1][3]. The reported profit metrics (ROE 20.48%, profit margin 68.77%) are entirely artifacts of the flyExclusive aviation business divestiture gain and do not reflect ongoing operations, which are deeply unprofitable. The company's D/E of 1% is the sole genuine financial strength — minimal debt provides some flexibility, but with a $2.64M market cap and negligible revenue, the balance sheet offers little comfort [4].
thesis_continued: The pivot to AI data center infrastructure via a 50MW LOI is aspirational at best — the company has no demonstrated expertise in data center operations, no construction capital, and no customer commitments, competing against operators with thousands of times more scale and capital (IREN has 3GW, hyperscalers have tens of GW) [2]. The 99.7% 52-week stock price decline, Altman Z-score of -0.58 (elevated bankruptcy risk), and NASDAQ compliance issues all indicate that JTAI faces existential risk [3][4]. The Inspire Impact Score of 0 (MIXED) reflects the absence of both positive and negative ESG attributions — the company is too small and unstable to have attracted meaningful ESG evaluation. This is not a turnaround story — it is a company with no viable path to profitability, no competitive advantages, and insufficient capital to execute its stated data center strategy.
key_catalysts: Successful execution of the 50MW data center project — if the company can secure financing, construction, and a customer for the facility, it could provide a viable revenue base, though this outcome is highly speculative given the company's $2.64M market cap and lack of infrastructure experience [2]

Completion of the flyExclusive aviation business divestiture could provide one-time cash proceeds and allow management to focus entirely on the data center strategy, removing the drag of an unprofitable legacy business [1]

A strategic acquirer or reverse merger partner could provide the capital and expertise needed to execute the data center strategy — the NASDAQ listing and clean balance sheet (minimal debt) have some residual shell value [3]
key_risks: Bankruptcy or NASDAQ delisting — the Altman Z-score of -0.58, $2.64M market cap, recurring NASDAQ minimum bid price violations, and history of two reverse splits in 18 months suggest the company may not survive as a going concern [3][4]

The 50MW data center pivot has no credible path to execution — the company lacks the capital, expertise, customer relationships, and operational infrastructure to build and operate a data center, competing against operators with billions in resources [2]

Ongoing shareholder dilution risk — the company's history of using equity issuances to fund operations, combined with the 1:200 reverse split making more shares available for issuance, suggests further dilution is likely if the company survives [3]
